egress.terms: Free, Cloudflare + Google Cloud CDN. Blob requests 307-redirect to cdn.registry.gitlab-static.net with a signed URL. Directly cacheable by an external Cloudflare zone.

record.tooling: Standard OCI Distribution v2. ORAS, skopeo, crane, docker. Auth flow is anonymous for public projects (`/jwt/auth` returns a token with auth_type=none).
record.chaining: One OCI artifact per blob of any size -> unlimited projects x unlimited repositories x unlimited tags. This is the canonical 'OCI registry as object store' pattern (ORAS). Blob dedupe means the same chunk stored in N projects costs one copy but is addressable N times.
record.limits_note: Auth token TTL 15 min on GitLab.com. Blob size limited only by the registry (manifest layers routinely are 100s of MB; no documented per-layer cap). Renaming a project with >1000 container repos is blocked. Public pulls are rate-limited loosely; anonymous token issuance works but each pull needs a token round-trip.
record.reliability_note: GitLab has run garbage-collection and cleanup-policy tooling against registries since 2023; no automatic purge is documented, but stale-tag cleanup policies are a first-class feature other users may set on shared projects. Own projects are not touched.

record.provider: GitLab Package Registry (generic / npm / Maven / PyPI / NuGet / Conan)

free_tier.stated: Explicitly EXCLUDED from the project storage quota. GitLab docs, verbatim: 'GitLab projects have a storage limit for their Git repository and Large File Storage (LFS). Only the project's repository and LFS are included in the storage limit. The container registry, package registry, and build artifacts are not included in the limit.' The 10 GiB figure (pricing page: 'Storage 10 GiB') therefore applies only to git+LFS; package bytes are unquota'd. Per-file ceilings: Generic 5 GB, npm 5 GB, Maven 5 GB, NuGet 5 GB, PyPI 5 GB, Conan 5 GB, Terraform 1 GB, ML model 10 GB (uploads capped at 5 GB), Helm 5 MB.

egress.terms: Free and unmetered for downloads; no egress line item anywhere in GitLab pricing. Served through Cloudflare (probe returned Server: cloudflare).

record.tooling: Full REST API: PUT /api/v4/projects/:id/packages/generic/:package_name/:version/:file_name and GET the same path for download. Package clients can target the GitLab registry URL directly. No rclone backend, but generic-package PUT and GET functions as a standard HTTP blob API. Deploy tokens with write_package_registry scope provide scoped push credentials.
record.chaining: GitLab Free permits unlimited projects per account with project creation limited to 200 per day per user. Generic packages allow up to 5 GB per file, and package registry storage is accounted separately from repository git limits.
record.limits_note: 5 GB per file (generic). Package registry rate limits apply to the Packages API. Authenticated API traffic 2,000 req/min per user; unauthenticated 60 req/hr per IP. Project creation 200/day/user. No per-project package storage cap documented.
record.reliability_note: Package registry is a real feature not a cache. No TTL, but a project cleanup policy can auto-delete package assets if configured, so leave it off. Anonymous pull must be enabled per project ('Allow anyone to pull from package registry'). NuGet group endpoints refuse anonymous pulls entirely.

record.notes: The GPU figure rests on one reading the pages do not settle. Usage is job duration / 60 x cost factor, runner type and project type sit in separate tables, and the project table gives public projects in the GitLab for Open Source program a cost factor of 0.5 with no runner qualifier. Read literally, a GPU job also costs 0.5, so 50,000 compute minutes are 100,000 job-minutes, or 1,667 GPU-hours a month. If the programme factor and the GPU runner factor of 7 multiply, 50,000 / 3.5 is 14,285 job-minutes, or 238 GPU-hours. The two readings differ by a factor of seven, and only a job run in an accepted namespace settles it. GPU runners are offered on Premium and Ultimate only, and the grant is Ultimate. The default runner is 2 vCPU and 8 GB, a job on GitLab.com hosted runners times out after 3 hours, and the grant is a monthly pool rather than unlimited time.

record.notes: The record is `card`, with a USD 1.00 authorisation hold and release. The pricing page's 'No credit card required' line is true of the account and false of the thing the record is about. GitLab's own FAQ says the card is required 'if you choose to use GitLab.com shared runners'. Shared runners are the only way to spend the 400 minutes without a self-managed runner. Identity verification on the GitLab free tier is a risk-scored three-stage scheme, and it is documented. Separately and unconditionally, the shared runners need a card. Not established: whether a new account from a given country lands in the medium-risk (phone) or high-risk (card) band, because the risk score is not published; and whether a debit or prepaid card passes the one-dollar authorisation, because no page says. The 400 minutes figure is confirmed.

free_tier.stated: 'The base monthly compute quota is determined by your subscription tier. Free tier namespaces receive 400 compute minutes per month.' The pricing page repeats it as '400 compute minutes per month'. A compute minute is not a wall-clock minute: the usage formula is 'Job duration / 60 * Cost factor', and the default `small` Linux x86-64 runner has cost factor 1, so 400 compute minutes is 400 wall-clock minutes on the default shape and less on any larger one. The card requirement is the finding: 'credit/debit card details are required if you choose to use GitLab.com shared runners', verified with 'a one-dollar authorization transaction'.
free_tier.notes: 400 compute minutes at cost factor 1 is 6 hours 40 minutes a month, which is 0.22 hours a day. The card gate is on the shared runners specifically, not on the account.

The card is verified by 'a one-dollar authorization transaction' and 'No charge will be made and no money will transfer', so the hold is USD 1.00 authorised and released, not captured. CONFIRMED: LFS is IN the quota while containers, packages, build artifacts, snippets, uploads and wikis are OUT.

egress.terms: Unmetered. GitLab does not bill or publish any LFS bandwidth quota. The only transfer-side control is a rate limit: 'Git LFS requests are subject to authenticated web request rate limits .. 1000 requests per minute per user. Each Git LFS object uploaded or downloaded generates an HTTP request'.

record.tooling: git-lfs. Also Oras-style raw access is not available; LFS is protocol-only. GitLab REST API v4 for project/namespace management (useful for automating project-per-shard).
record.chaining: 10 GiB per PROJECT, and projects are free and unlimited within a namespace. GitLab's own excess-storage example totals 30 GiB across three projects with no namespace-level cap. 50 projects = 500 GiB, 100 = 1 TiB. This is the cleanest 'trivially repeatable' LFS case because each project is an independent 10 GiB bucket behind the same account, unlike GitHub where the 10 GiB is per account.
record.limits_note: At 10 GiB the project goes READ-ONLY: 'you can't push or add large files (LFS) to the project's repository.' Max push request 5 GiB (through Cloudflare). This applies to git push; LFS object upload is a separate endpoint. Max attachment 100 MiB. Rate limit 1000 LFS req/min/user is the real throughput ceiling (~60k objects/hour, and one object = one request regardless of size).
record.reliability_note: Read-only state is reversible only by purchasing storage, so a blown project is stuck. The 1000 req/min limit bites hard on many-small-files datasets during clone, and GitLab's own docs warn multi-file projects 'may encounter an HTTP rate limit error' in CI.
